s.line: After a few hours the road began to be rough,
s.note: דֶּרֶךְ מְשֻׁבֶּשֶׁת = a bumpy, broken-up road. מְשֻׁבָּשׁ is a pu'al participle, "disrupted, garbled". You'll hear it in traffic news (הַתְּנוּעָה מְשֻׁבֶּשֶׁת, traffic is disrupted) and of bad language (עִבְרִית מְשֻׁבֶּשֶׁת, broken Hebrew). דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine, hence הִתְחִילָה.

w: לְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת|often|~idiom: lit. at near times
s.line: and the walking grew so difficult that the Scarecrow often stumbled over the yellow bricks, which were here very uneven.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = became: נַעֲשָׂה קַר (it got cold). מֻנָּח is the hof'al participle of הֵנִיחַ (to put, lay down): "placed, lying". Everyday: הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת מֻנָּחִים עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן (the keys are on the table).

s.line: Sometimes, indeed, they were broken or missing altogether, leaving holes that Toto jumped across and Dorothy walked around.
s.note: עָקַף = to go around something; on the road it means "to overtake": הוּא עָקַף אֶת הַמַּשָּׂאִית. A detour is עֲקִיפָה or מַעֲקָף. חָסַר = to be missing: חָסֵר לִי כֶּסֶף (I'm short of money).

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
לְכָל אָרְכּוֹ|at full length|~idiom: lit. to all his length
s.line: As for the Scarecrow, having no brains, he walked straight ahead, and so stepped into the holes and fell at full length on the hard bricks.
s.note: וְאִלּוּ = "whereas, while (by contrast)", the usual way to set one person against another: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב קָפֶה, וְאִלּוּ הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת תֵּה. דָּרַךְ = to step on (דָּרַכְתָּ לִי עַל הָרֶגֶל, you stepped on my foot); the same root gives דֶּרֶךְ, road.

s.line: It never hurt him, however,
s.note: כָּאַב לוֹ = it hurt him: the thing that hurts is the subject, and the person gets לְ. כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ = my head hurts / I have a headache.

s.line: and Dorothy would pick him up and set him upon his feet again, while he joined her in laughing merrily at his own mishap.
s.note: הָיְתָה מְרִימָה: past of הָיָה + participle = "used to / would" for something that happened again and again, exactly like Baum's "would pick him up". הֶעֱמִיד (hif'il of עָמַד, to stand) = to stand someone up, make him stand. תַּקָּלָה = a hitch, a glitch; it is also the word for a technical fault: תַּקָּלָה בַּמַּעֲרֶכֶת.

s.line: The farms were not nearly so well cared for here as they were farther back.
s.note: מְטֻפָּח (pu'al participle) = well-kept, groomed. It is used of gardens and of people: הִיא תָּמִיד מְטֻפַּחַת (she is always well-groomed). The pi'el טִפֵּחַ = to cultivate, nurture.

s.line: There were fewer houses and fewer fruit trees,

w: וּכְכָל שֶׁ|and the more that|~idiom: the more … the more
s.line: and the farther they went the more dismal and lonesome the country became.
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ… כָּךְ … = "the more … the more": כְּכָל שֶׁתִּתְאַמֵּן יוֹתֵר, כָּךְ תִּהְיֶה טוֹב יוֹתֵר (the more you practice, the better you'll be). In speech the כָּךְ is often dropped. שׁוֹמֵם = deserted, desolate: רְחוֹב שׁוֹמֵם.

s.line: At noon they sat down by the roadside, near a little brook,
s.note: הִתְיַשֵּׁב (hitpa'el) = sat down, the movement; יָשַׁב (pa'al) = sat, was sitting. הִתְיַשֵּׁב also means "to settle (a land)", which gives הִתְיַשְּׁבוּת (settlement) and יִשּׁוּב (a community, village).

s.line: and Dorothy opened her basket and got out some bread.
She offered a piece to the Scarecrow, but he refused.
s.note: הִצִּיעַ = to offer, propose; הַצָּעָה = an offer, a proposal (also a marriage proposal). סֵרֵב = to refuse, usually + לְ + infinitive: הוּא סֵרֵב לֶאֱכֹל. The noun is סֵרוּב.

s.line: “I am never hungry,” he said, “and it is a lucky thing I am not,
s.note: זֶה מַזָּל שֶׁ… / מַזָּל שֶׁ… = "it's lucky that …, good thing that …": מַזָּל שֶׁבָּאתָ (good thing you came). לֹא on its own stands for the whole clause "that I am not (hungry)".

s.line: for my mouth is only painted,
and if I should cut a hole in it so I could eat, the straw I am stuffed with would come out, and that would spoil the shape of my head.”
s.note: Two pu'al participles in a row, both passives of pi'el verbs: צִיֵּר painted → מְצֻיָּר painted (drawn); מִלֵּא filled → מְמֻלָּא stuffed, filled. In the kitchen, מְמֻלָּאִים are stuffed vegetables. קִלְקֵל = to spoil, break; מְקֻלְקָל = broken, out of order.

s.line: Dorothy saw at once that this was true, so she only nodded and went on eating her bread.
s.note: רָאֲתָה שֶׁזֶּה נָכוֹן: after "see, know, say", Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought, so "saw that it was true" is literally "saw that it is true". הִמְשִׁיךְ + infinitive = to go on doing: תַּמְשִׁיךְ לְדַבֵּר (keep talking).

s.line: “Tell me something about yourself and the country you came from,” said the Scarecrow, when she had finished her dinner.
s.note: סַפְּרִי is the feminine imperative (to a man סַפֵּר). עַצְמֵךְ = yourself (fem.); עַצְמְךָ to a man. Hebrew has no past perfect: "had finished" is plain סִיְּמָה.

s.line: So she told him all about Kansas, and how gray everything was there, and how the cyclone had carried her to this queer Land of Oz.
s.note: נָשָׂא = to carry, a little bookish; in speech you'd more often say לָקַח or סָחַב. It also means "to marry (a wife)" and, in the news, "to deliver (a speech)": נָשָׂא נְאוּם. אֶרֶץ is feminine, so הַמּוּזָרָה הַזֹּאת.

s.line: The Scarecrow listened carefully, and said,
s.note: תְּשׂוּמַת לֵב = attention ("placing of the heart"). שִׂים לֵב! = pay attention! / watch out!, one of the most common phrases in Hebrew. הִקְשִׁיב לְ… = to listen to.

s.line: “I cannot understand why you should wish to leave this beautiful country and go back to the dry, gray place you call Kansas.”
s.note: קָרָא לְ… = to call (name) something: אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ? = what's your name? (lit. how do they call you?). Without לְ, קָרָא = to read or to call out.

w: אֵין לְךָ|you have no|~lit. there is not to you
s.line: “That is because you have no brains” answered the girl.

w: לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה|no matter|~idiom: lit. it doesn't change
כְּכָל שֶׁתִּהְיֶה|however it may be|~idiom: as much as it will be
s.line: “No matter how dreary and gray our homes are, we people of flesh and blood would rather live there than in any other country, be it ever so beautiful.
s.note: לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה = "it doesn't matter, no matter …", and on its own "never mind": לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה, עֲזֹב. בָּשָׂר וָדָם = flesh and blood, an ordinary mortal, as in English. הֶעֱדִיף = to prefer; עֲדִיף = it's better: עֲדִיף לְחַכּוֹת.

w: אֵין כְּמוֹ בַּבַּיִת|there's no place like home|~idiom: lit. there's nothing like at home
s.line: There is no place like home.”
The Scarecrow sighed.
s.note: נֶאֱנַח = sighed: nif'al in form, but active in meaning. The noun is אֲנָחָה, and אַנְחַת רְוָחָה is a sigh of relief, a favorite phrase of news writers.

w: בָּרוּר שֶׁ|of course|~idiom: it's clear that
s.line: “Of course I cannot understand it,” he said.
“If your heads were stuffed with straw, like mine, you would probably all live in the beautiful places, and then Kansas would have no people at all.
s.note: An unreal "if": אִלּוּ + past, then הָיָה + participle for "would": הֱיִיתֶם גָּרִים = you would live. In speech אִם is often used instead of אִלּוּ. כַּנִּרְאֶה = probably, apparently ("as it seems"), from the same root as נִרְאֶה.

w: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָכֶם|that you have|~lit. that there is to you
s.line: It is fortunate for Kansas that you have brains.”
“Won’t you tell me a story, while we are resting?” asked the child.
s.note: אוּלַי תְּ…? + future = a soft, polite request: אוּלַי תַּעֲזֹר לִי? (could you help me?). סִפֵּר (to tell) and סִפּוּר (a story) share the root ס־פ־ר with סֵפֶר (book) and מִסְפָּר (number).

s.line: The Scarecrow looked at her reproachfully, and answered:
s.note: נָזַף בְּ… = to scold, rebuke; נְזִיפָה = a reprimand, also the official word in army and workplace news (הוּא קִבֵּל נְזִיפָה). הִבִּיט בְּ… takes בְּ, so "at her" is בָּהּ.

s.line: “My life has been so short that I really know nothing whatever.
s.note: חַיִּים (life) is always plural in Hebrew, so the verb and adjective are plural too: הַחַיִּים הָיוּ קְצָרִים. Same with מַיִם (water) and פָּנִים (face).

s.line: I was only made day before yesterday.
s.note: עָשׂוּ אוֹתִי ("they made me") with no subject is the everyday Hebrew way to say "I was made". שִׁלְשׁוֹם = the day before yesterday; the day after tomorrow is מָחֳרָתַיִם.

s.line: What happened in the world before that time is all unknown to me.
s.note: מֻכָּר = known, familiar: the hof'al participle of הִכִּיר (to know a person or place). זֶה נִשְׁמָע לִי מֻכָּר = that sounds familiar. לִפְנֵי כֵן = before that, earlier.

s.line: Luckily, when the farmer made my head, one of the first things he did was to paint my ears, so that I heard what was going on.
s.note: לְמַזָּלִי = luckily (for me); לְמַזָּלָהּ for her, לְמַרְבֶּה הַמַּזָּל = fortunately. מָה קוֹרֶה = what's happening, and on its own the everyday greeting "what's up?".

s.line: There was another Munchkin with him,

w: מָה דַּעְתְּךָ עַל|what do you think of|~idiom: lit. what is your opinion on
s.line: and the first thing I heard was the farmer saying, ‘How do you like those ears?’
s.note: מָה דַּעְתְּךָ עַל …? = what do you think of …? / how do you like …? (to a woman מָה דַּעְתֵּךְ). דֵּעָה = opinion, and לְדַעְתִּי = in my opinion.

s.line: “‘They aren’t straight,’” answered the other.
s.note: אֹזֶן (ear), like most paired body parts (עַיִן, יָד, רֶגֶל), is feminine, so הֵן … יְשָׁרוֹת. הַשֵּׁנִי = "the second", and so "the other one" when there are two.

w: לֹא נוֹרָא|never mind|~idiom: lit. not terrible
s.line: “‘Never mind,’” said the farmer.
s.note: לֹא נוֹרָא = never mind, no big deal, it's OK: what you say when someone apologizes for a small thing. נוֹרָא alone = terrible, awful, and in speech also "terribly": נוֹרָא חַם (it's awfully hot).

s.line: “‘They are ears just the same,’” which was true enough.
“‘Now I’ll make the eyes,’” said the farmer.
So he painted my right eye,

w: וּבְרֶגַע שֶׁ|and as soon as|~idiom: lit. in the moment that
s.line: and as soon as it was finished I found myself looking at him and at everything around me with a great deal of curiosity,
s.note: הֻשְׁלַם = was completed: hof'al, the passive of הִשְׁלִים (to complete). Also הִשְׁלִים עִם = to come to terms with. הִסְתַּכֵּל עַל = to look at (with עַל), while הִבִּיט takes בְּ. In hitpa'el, the ת swaps places with a first root letter ס: הִסְתַּכֵּל, not הִתְסַכֵּל.

s.line: for this was my first glimpse of the world.
“‘That’s a rather pretty eye,’” remarked the Munchkin who was watching the farmer.
s.note: צָפָה בְּ… = to watch: צָפִיתִי בַּסֶּרֶט (I watched the film); a viewer is צוֹפֶה. Hebrew uses the simple past צָפָה for English "was watching".

s.line: “‘Blue paint is just the color for eyes.’
s.note: צֶבַע means both "color" and "paint", which makes the farmer's line neat in Hebrew. מַתְאִים = suitable, right for: זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי = that doesn't suit me / that's not a good time for me.

s.line: “‘I think I’ll make the other a little bigger,’” said the farmer.
s.note: שֶׁאֶת הַשְּׁנִיָּה אֶעֱשֶׂה: the object comes first, for contrast ("the other one, I'll make bigger"), a very common move in spoken Hebrew. הַשְּׁנִיָּה is feminine because עַיִן is.

s.line: And when the second eye was done I could see much better than before.
s.note: מוּכָן = ready, is in form a hof'al participle of הֵכִין (to prepare): "prepared". אַתָּה מוּכָן? = are you ready? It also means "willing": אֲנִי מוּכָן לַעֲזֹר.

s.line: Then he made my nose and my mouth.
But I did not speak, because at that time I didn’t know what a mouth was for.
s.note: שִׁמֵּשׁ לְ… = to serve as, be used for: הַחֶדֶר מְשַׁמֵּשׁ כְּמִשְׂרָד (the room is used as an office). Related: שִׁמּוּשׁ (use) and שִׁמּוּשִׁי (useful). Don't confuse לְמָה "for what" with לָמָּה "why".

s.line: I had the fun of watching them make my body and my arms and legs;
s.note: נֶהֱנָה = enjoyed, a nif'al with active meaning, + infinitive or מִ…: נֶהֱנֵיתִי מֵהַהַצָּגָה (I enjoyed the show). You'll hear תֵּהָנֶה! = enjoy! all the time. יָד in Hebrew covers both the hand and the whole arm.

s.line: and when they fastened on my head, at last, I felt very proud, for I thought I was just as good a man as anyone.
s.note: חִבֵּר = to attach, connect (חִבַּרְתִּי אֶת הַמַּטְעֵן, I plugged in the charger); it also means "to add" in arithmetic and "to compose" a book. סוֹף סוֹף = finally, at last.

s.line: “‘This fellow will scare the crows fast enough,’ said the farmer.
s.note: A binyan pair: בָּרַח (pa'al) = to run away, flee; הִבְרִיחַ (hif'il) = to make someone run away, chase off. הִבְרִיחַ is also the news word for "to smuggle": הִבְרִיחוּ סִחוֹרָה, and a smuggler is a מַבְרִיחַ.

s.line: ‘He looks just like a man.’
“‘Why, he is a man,’ said the other,
s.note: הֲרֵי = "why, but surely, after all": it presents something as obvious. הֲרֵי אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ! = but I told you! It is also a reasoning word, "since": שֶׁהֲרֵי.

s.line: and I quite agreed with him.
s.note: הִסְכִּים עִם = to agree with someone; הִסְכִּים לְ… = to agree to something. הֶסְכֵּם = an agreement, the standard news word for a treaty or deal (הֶסְכֵּם שָׁלוֹם).

s.line: The farmer carried me under his arm to the cornfield, and set me up on a tall stick, where you found me.
s.note: שֶׁבּוֹ = "in which", the standard way to say "where" after a noun: הַבַּיִת שֶׁבּוֹ גָּדַלְתִּי (the house where I grew up). In speech people often just say אֵיפֹה שֶׁ…. מָצָאת is "you found" said to a girl or woman.

s.line: He and his friend soon after walked away and left me alone.
s.note: הִשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something or someone behind, and its partner נִשְׁאַר (nif'al) = to stay, remain. תַּשְׁאִיר לִי הוֹדָעָה = leave me a message.

s.line: “I did not like to be deserted this way.
s.note: נָטַשׁ = to abandon, desert; its pa'ul form נָטוּשׁ = abandoned: בַּיִת נָטוּשׁ, כֶּלֶב נָטוּשׁ. Again "they deserted me" (no subject) stands for the English passive "to be deserted".

s.line: So I tried to walk after them.
But my feet would not touch the ground, and I was forced to stay on that pole.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ = was forced to, had to: a nif'al with real passive meaning and a slightly formal, newsy feel (הַטַּיָּס נֶאֱלַץ לִנְחֹת, the pilot was forced to land). In conversation you'd say הָיִיתִי חַיָּב. לְהִשָּׁאֵר is the nif'al infinitive of נִשְׁאַר.

w: הָיוּ לִי|I had|~lit. there were to me
לֹא מִזְּמַן|recently|~idiom: lit. not from long ago
s.line: It was a lonely life to lead, for I had nothing to think of, having been made such a little while before.
s.note: לֹא הָיָה לִי עַל מָה לַחְשֹׁב = "I had nothing to think about", literally "I didn't have about-what to think". The pattern is common: אֵין לִי מָה לַעֲשׂוֹת (I have nothing to do), אֵין עַל מָה (you're welcome, lit. there's nothing for which [to thank]). נוֹצַר = was created, the nif'al passive of יָצַר.

s.line: Many crows and other birds flew into the cornfield, but as soon as they saw me they flew away again, thinking I was a Munchkin;
s.note: צִפּוֹר is feminine (צִפּוֹרִים אֲחֵרוֹת), even though its plural ends in ִים. With a mixed group, crows (masc.) and birds (fem.), Hebrew uses the masculine: הֵם עָפוּ.

w: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי|pleased me|~idiom: lit. found favor in my eyes
s.line: and this pleased me and made me feel that I was quite an important person.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ… + infinitive = to make, cause someone to: זֶה גָּרַם לִי לִצְחֹק (it made me laugh). גּוֹרֵם = a factor; in the news גּוֹרְמִים בַּמִּשְׂרָד = "sources in the ministry".

s.line: By and by an old crow flew near me,
and after looking at me carefully he perched upon my shoulder and said:
s.note: נָחַת = to land, used of birds and planes: הַמָּטוֹס נָחַת. Landing is נְחִיתָה, take-off הַמְרָאָה. הֵיטֵב = well, thoroughly, a bit more formal than טוֹב: תַּקְשִׁיבוּ הֵיטֵב.

s.line: “‘I wonder if that farmer thought to fool me in this clumsy manner.
s.note: מְעַנְיֵן אִם … = I wonder if … (lit. "it's interesting whether"). רִמָּה = to cheat, fool; the Wizard will later be called a רַמַּאי, from the same root. תַּרְגִּיל = a trick, ploy, but also an exercise (in school or the gym). מְגֻשָּׁם = clumsy, crude.

s.line: Any crow of sense could see that you are only stuffed with straw.’
s.note: נָבוֹן = wise, sensible, a nif'al participle from the root ב־י־ן, like הֵבִין (understood) and מֵבִין. הַחְלָטָה נְבוֹנָה = a wise decision.

s.line: Then he hopped down at my feet and ate all the corn he wanted.
s.note: קִפֵּץ (pi'el) = to hop, skip, bounce around; קָפַץ (pa'al) = to jump, one jump. The pi'el often adds repetition like this. כַּמָּה שֶׁ… = as much as: קַח כַּמָּה שֶׁאַתָּה רוֹצֶה (take as much as you want).

s.line: The other birds, seeing he was not harmed by me, came to eat the corn too,
s.note: נִפְגַּע = was hurt, harmed: the nif'al passive of פָּגַע בְּ… (to hit, hurt). Very common in the news: אִישׁ לֹא נִפְגַּע (no one was hurt), נִפְגָּעִים (casualties). It is also "offended": הוּא נִפְגַּע = his feelings were hurt.

s.line: so in a short time there was a great flock of them about me.
s.note: לַהֲקָה = a flock of birds, but also a band or performing troupe: לַהֲקַת רוֹק, לַהֲקָה צְבָאִית (an army entertainment troupe). הִתְאַסֵּף = to gather, assemble; אֲסֵפָה = a meeting.

w: שֶׁבְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר|that after all|~idiom: lit. at the end of the matter
s.line: “I felt sad at this, for it showed I was not such a good Scarecrow after all;
s.note: Two hif'il verbs that mean "to cause": עָצוּב sad → הֶעֱצִיב to make sad; רָאָה saw → הֶרְאָה to show (make see). בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר = in the end, after all, a set phrase.

w: הָיָה לְךָ|you had|~lit. there was to you
s.line: but the old crow comforted me, saying, ‘If you only had brains in your head you would be as good a man as any of them, and a better man than some of them.
s.note: לוּ רַק … = if only …, a wish or unreal condition (like אִלּוּ). With a noun after it, plain הָיִיתָ already means "you would be". נִחֵם = to comfort, console; נֶחָמָה = comfort. The mourners' formula הַמָּקוֹם יְנַחֵם comes from the same verb.

w: שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְךָ|you having|~lit. that there will be to you
s.line: Brains are the only things worth having in this world, no matter whether one is a crow or a man.’
s.note: שָׁוֶה = worth: זֶה שָׁוֶה אֶת זֶה (it's worth it), זֶה לֹא שָׁוֶה כְּלוּם (it's worthless). It also means "equal": שָׁוֶה בְּשָׁוֶה = fifty-fifty. Hebrew uses אַתָּה for a general "one" or "you".

s.line: “After the crows had gone I thought this over, and decided I would try hard to get some brains.
s.note: הִשְׁתַּדֵּל = to try hard, make an effort; another hitpa'el where the ת swaps with the first root letter (here שׂ), as in הִסְתַּכֵּל. הִשִּׂיג = to get, obtain, achieve: קָשֶׁה לְהַשִּׂיג כַּרְטִיסִים (tickets are hard to get).

s.line: By good luck you came along and pulled me off the stake,
s.note: הוֹרִיד (hif'il of יָרַד, went down) = to take down, lower; also "to download": הוֹרַדְתִּי אֶת הָאַפְּלִיקַצְיָה. The ending ְתְּ (הִגַּעְתְּ, הוֹרַדְתְּ) marks "you" to a woman or girl.

s.line: and from what you say I am sure the Great Oz will give me brains as soon as we get to the Emerald City.”
“I hope so,” said Dorothy earnestly, “since you seem anxious to have them.”
s.note: מְקַוֶּה שֶׁכֵּן = I hope so; מְקַוֶּה שֶׁלֹּא = I hope not. Dorothy says מְקַוָּה, the feminine form. תִּקְוָה (hope) is from the same root; Israel's anthem is הַתִּקְוָה.

s.line: “Oh, yes; I am anxious,” returned the Scarecrow.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב = replied, a literary alternative to עָנָה. Like English "returned", it also means "to give back": הוּא הֵשִׁיב אֶת הַכֶּסֶף. תְּשׁוּבָה (answer) comes from the same root שׁ־ו־ב (return).

s.line: “It is such an uncomfortable feeling to know one is a fool.”
s.note: לֹא נָעִים = unpleasant, uncomfortable, and in speech also "embarrassing": לֹא נָעִים לִי לְבַקֵּשׁ (I feel awkward asking). זוֹ is the feminine "this/it is", matching הַרְגָּשָׁה; in speech you'll hear זֹאת too.

s.line: “Well,” said the girl, “let us go.”
s.note: בּוֹא נֵלֵךְ = let's go: "come" + future "we". Said to a girl it's בּוֹאִי נֵלֵךְ, to a group בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ. טוֹב at the start of a sentence = "OK, well, right".

s.line: And she handed the basket to the Scarecrow.
s.note: מָסַר = to hand over, pass: in football, מָסַר is to pass the ball (מְסִירָה, a pass). תִּמְסֹר לוֹ דְּרִישַׁת שָׁלוֹם = give him my regards. מֶסֶר = a message.

s.line: There were no fences at all by the roadside now, and the land was rough and untilled.
s.note: מְעֻבָּד (pu'al participle of עִבֵּד) = cultivated (land), and also "processed": מָזוֹן מְעֻבָּד (processed food), עִבּוּד נְתוּנִים (data processing). בִּלְתִּי = "un-, non-", a more formal negative before adjectives: בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁרִי = impossible.

w: דֶּרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|the yellow brick road
s.line: Toward evening they came to a great forest, where the trees grew so big and close together that their branches met over the road of yellow brick.
s.note: נִפְגַּשׁ = to meet: a nif'al with a "each other" sense, not a passive. נִפְגַּשְׁנוּ בַּקָּפֶה = we met at the café; פְּגִישָׁה = a meeting. צָפוּף = crowded, dense, packed: הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס הָיָה צָפוּף.

s.line: It was almost dark under the trees, for the branches shut out the daylight;
s.note: חָסַם = to block: הַכְּבִישׁ חָסוּם (the road is closed), and מַחְסוֹם is a barrier or roadblock, a word heard daily on Israeli radio. On a phone, חָסַמְתִּי אוֹתוֹ = I blocked him.

s.line: but the travelers did not stop, and went on into the forest.
“If this road goes in, it must come out,” said the Scarecrow,
“and as the Emerald City is at the other end of the road, we must go wherever it leads us.”
s.note: נִמְצָא = is located, is (somewhere): אֵיפֹה נִמְצֵאת הַתַּחֲנָה? (where is the station?). Its old passive sense "was found" survives in נִמְצָא in the news. מִכֵּיוָן שֶׁ = since, because, a little more formal than כִּי.

s.line: “Anyone would know that,” said Dorothy.
“Certainly; that is why I know it,” returned the Scarecrow.
“If it required brains to figure it out, I never should have said it.”
s.note: פִּצֵּחַ = to crack: nuts and sunflower seeds (לְפַצֵּחַ גַּרְעִינִים, the Israeli pastime), and, figuratively, a code, a riddle or a case (הַמִּשְׁטָרָה פִּצְּחָה אֶת הַתַּעֲלוּמָה). הָיִיתִי אוֹמֵר = "I would say", the unreal result again.

s.line: After an hour or so the light faded away, and they found themselves stumbling along in the darkness.
s.note: דָּעַךְ = to fade, die down (a fire, a light), and in the news: הַמְּחָאָה דּוֹעֶכֶת (the protest is dying down). בְּעֵרֶךְ = about, approximately, placed after or before the number: שָׁעָה בְּעֵרֶךְ / בְּעֵרֶךְ שָׁעָה.

s.line: Dorothy could not see at all, but Toto could, for some dogs see very well in the dark;
s.note: יֵשׁ כְּלָבִים שֶׁ… = "some dogs …", literally "there are dogs that …": יֵשׁ אֲנָשִׁים שֶׁאוֹהֲבִים חֹרֶף (some people like winter). Note the past "could": יָכְלָה for Dorothy, יָכֹל for Toto.

s.line: and the Scarecrow declared he could see as well as by day.
s.note: הִכְרִיז = to declare, announce, a high-frequency news verb: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל … (the government announced …). The noun is הַכְרָזָה; כָּרוֹז = a public notice or town crier.

s.line: So she took hold of his arm and managed to get along fairly well.
s.note: אָחַז בְּ… = to grip, hold on to, with בְּ. הִצְלִיחַ = to succeed, and + infinitive "to manage to": הִצְלַחְתִּי לִישֹׁן (I managed to sleep). בְּהַצְלָחָה! = good luck!

s.line: “If you see any house, or any place where we can pass the night,” she said, “you must tell me;
s.note: בִּלָּה = to spend (time): בִּלִּינוּ שָׁבוּעַ בְּאֵילַת. On its own it means "to have a good time, go out": יָצָאנוּ לְבַלּוֹת, and בִּלּוּי = an outing, entertainment. כָּלְשֶׁהוּ = any, some (or other).

s.line: for it is very uncomfortable walking in the dark.”
Soon after the Scarecrow stopped.
s.note: נֶעֱצַר = came to a stop (himself), while עָצַר = to stop something or someone. In the news נֶעֱצַר is a real passive: הַחָשׁוּד נֶעֱצַר = the suspect was arrested.

w: מִיָּמִין לָנוּ|on our right|~idiom: lit. from right to us
s.line: “I see a little cottage at the right of us,” he said, “built of logs and branches.
s.note: בָּנוּי = built: the pa'ul participle of בָּנָה, a passive form you see on signs and in descriptions (בָּנוּי מֵאֶבֶן, built of stone). בִּקְתָּה = a hut, cabin. מִיָּמִין / מִשְּׂמֹאל = on the right / on the left.

s.line: Shall we go there?”
“Yes, indeed,” answered the child.
“I am all tired out.”
s.note: אֲנִי גָּמוּר / גְּמוּרָה = "I'm exhausted, I'm done for", everyday slang built on the pa'ul form of גָּמַר (to finish). בְּהֶחְלֵט = definitely, absolutely, a common emphatic "yes".

s.line: So the Scarecrow led her through the trees until they reached the cottage,
and Dorothy entered and found a bed of dried leaves in one corner.
She lay down at once, and with Toto beside her soon fell into a sound sleep.
s.note: נִשְׁכַּב (nif'al) = to lie down, the movement; שָׁכַב (pa'al) = to be lying. Compare הִתְיַשֵּׁב / יָשַׁב earlier in this chapter. שָׁקַע בְּשֵׁנָה = fell fast asleep; שָׁקַע = to sink, and שְׁקִיעָה = sunset.

s.line: The Scarecrow, who was never tired, stood up in another corner and waited patiently until morning came.
s.note: חִכָּה = to wait, + לְ… for the person or thing: חִכִּיתִי לְךָ (I waited for you). רַק רֶגַע, תְּחַכֶּה! = just a moment, wait! בְּסַבְלָנוּת = patiently; סַבְלָן = patient.
